detail:
The National Institute of Dental and Craniofacial Research (NIDCR) describes trigeminal neuralgia (TN), also called tic douloureux, as a chronic pain condition affecting the trigeminal nerve, the nerve responsible for sensation in the face, including the mouth. TN causes episodes of sudden, extreme pain described as electric shock-like, shooting, stabbing, or sharp, typically on one side of the face. In type 1 TN the pain comes in brief attacks, while people with type 2 TN can have constant aching, burning, and stabbing pain that is usually less severe.

TN may be caused by a blood vessel pressing on the trigeminal nerve, and when other diseases cause it, the condition is called secondary trigeminal neuralgia; causes can include multiple sclerosis, other inflammatory diseases, and a brain tumor or tangle of abnormal blood vessels compressing the nerve. The condition occurs most often in people over age 50, although it can occur at any age, and it is more common in women. Although the pain is not life threatening, NIDCR notes it can be physically and mentally disabling.

Tabs is not endorsing or verifying this material. Talk to your doctor about trigeminal neuralgia symptoms and diagnosis.

a blood vessel pressing on the nerve is a common cause described

title: Trigeminal Neuralgia: sudden, shock-like facial pain
